country.name: Australia
country.summary: Australia is a federation of climates, not one hot country. Vines sit in a crescent along the southern rim of the continent, and coolness is hunted down by height, by sea air or by latitude. South Australia grows the most and has never known phylloxera, so ungrafted Shiraz planted in the 1840s still crops in the Barossa. The law describes origin only: a Geographical Indication draws a line on a map and promises no grape, no yield and no style, and the one rule a server must hold is 85 per cent, for variety, for vintage and for region, with blends named in descending order. Shiraz leads the plantings and Chardonnay the whites. The exam's favourite pairs are Barossa against Coonawarra, Grange against Hill of Grace, and Clare's bone-dry Riesling against the German expectation of sweetness.
country.overview:
The first vines came ashore with the First Fleet at Sydney Cove in 1788, and the cuttings James Busby collected in Europe in 1831 and landed in 1832 seeded much of what followed. The Barossa was settled from 1842 by Silesian Lutherans and English farmers, and the houses a server still pours date from that decade and the next: Penfolds in 1844, Yalumba in 1849, Seppeltsfield in 1851. For a century the trade was mostly fortified wine. The turn to table wine came after the Second World War, and the first experimental Grange of 1951 marks it. The export boom of the 1980s and 1990s built the big companies and a name for ripe, friendly, varietally labelled wine; since then the task has been proving that the regions differ.

They differ because the continent does. The interior is desert, the north tropical, so wine lives in a southern crescent from Margaret River to the Hunter and Tasmania. Rain falls mostly in winter, so irrigation is normal. Three hot irrigated districts along the Murray and the Murrumbidgee, the Riverland, the Murray Darling with Swan Hill, and the Riverina, grow the bulk of everyday wine. Coolness comes from altitude at Clare, Eden Valley and Orange, from the sea at Margaret River and McLaren Vale, and from latitude in Tasmania. South Australia inspects traffic at its border because phylloxera never crossed it; Western Australia and Tasmania are free as well, while pockets of Victoria and New South Wales are not.

The law is a map. Geographical Indications were written into the national wine legislation in the early 1990s, after Australia agreed with the European Community to give up European names. A zone groups regions and proves nothing; a region must be one tract with five independently owned vineyards of five hectares and a usual crop of 500 tonnes, measurably discrete and measurably homogeneous in its grape growing; a subregion passes the same size test and must be substantially discrete and substantially homogeneous. No tier carries a rule on grape, yield, ageing or taste. The Label Integrity Programme, in force since 1990, audits the claims through winery records: a named variety, vintage or GI must be at least 85 per cent of the wine, named varieties are listed in descending order and together make 85 per cent, and up to three GIs may be named at 95 per cent in all. Hermitage, Burgundy and Champagne left Australian labels under the first agreement; Sherry, Tokay and Port followed in 2010, becoming Apera, Topaque and Tawny. Langton’s is a private auction-house classification, not law.

The exam leans on the signatures. Barossa Shiraz from ancient own-rooted vines, Coonawarra Cabernet on terra rossa, Clare and Eden Riesling dry under screwcap, Margaret River Cabernet and Chardonnay with sea-tempered poise, Hunter Semillon picked early and transformed by bottle age, Rutherglen’s raisined Muscat, and Tasmania’s sparkling base and Pinot Noir. Hold Grange and Hill of Grace apart, read a blend’s name in order, and remember a GI is only a place.
ladder: The smallest GI, lying inside a region: it passes the same size test as a region and must be substantially discrete and substantially homogeneous in its grape growing. High Eden inside Eden Valley is the exam's example; the Margaret River districts are not registered.

The working unit, Barossa Valley or Coonawarra: one tract of land with at least five independently owned vineyards of five hectares each, usually cropping at least 500 tonnes a year, measurably discrete from its neighbours and measurably homogeneous in its grape growing.

A grouping of regions with no homogeneity required: Barossa holds Barossa Valley and Eden Valley, Limestone Coast holds Coonawarra and five neighbours, Fleurieu holds McLaren Vale, Mount Lofty Ranges holds Clare Valley and the Adelaide Hills.

Each state is a GI in its own right, and South Eastern Australia is the super-zone that takes New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania whole with the grape-growing parts of Queensland and South Australia: the origin on most blended export wine.
labels: 85 per cent
A stated variety, vintage or GI must be at least 85 per cent of the wine.
Shiraz Cabernet
Named varieties are listed in descending order, together make at least 85 per cent, and each named grape outweighs any unnamed one; the first word is the larger share.
Blend of GIs
Up to three regions may be named in descending order, together at least 95 per cent of the wine and each at least 5 per cent.
Bin number
A house code such as Penfolds Bin 389 or Bin 707: no legal meaning at all.
Old Vine
Unregulated in national law; the Barossa's own charter defines Old, Survivor, Centenarian and Ancestor vines at 35, 70, 100 and 125 years.
Show Reserve
A marketing term that points at wine-show medals, not a legal tier.
Apera, Topaque, Tawny
The names that replaced Sherry, Tokay and Port on Australian fortified wine when the agreement with the European Union took effect in 2010.
Langton's
A private classification of collectible wines in tiers of Exceptional, Outstanding and Excellent, revised periodically; not law.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The most planted grape and the national red: broad, chocolatey and ripe on the Barossa floor, savoury and saline in McLaren Vale, earthy and medium-bodied in the Hunter, peppery in cool Victoria.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The leading white, grown everywhere from the hot inland to Tasmania; the modern style is leaner, earlier picked and barrel fermented, with Margaret River, the Yarra and the Adelaide Hills setting the pace.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Most structured on Coonawarra's terra rossa and most Bordeaux-like in Margaret River; often blended with Shiraz in South Australia, a pairing France never made.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Dry by default, lime and slate, high in acid and bottled under screwcap: Clare and Eden Valley are the homes, with Great Southern and Tasmania behind them.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: The Hunter's strange glory, picked at low alcohol, unoaked and transformed by bottle age into toast and lanolin; blended with Sauvignon Blanc in Margaret River and botrytised in the Riverina.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: Old bush vines in the Barossa and McLaren Vale, once fortified fodder, now perfumed mid-weight reds and the G of GSM.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.styles: Called Mataro in South Australia: dark, meaty and tannic, the M of GSM and a minor varietal from old vines.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: At home only where it is cool: the Yarra, Mornington, the Adelaide Hills and Tasmania, and the base of the best sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Mostly a blending partner for Cabernet in Margaret River and Coonawarra, rarely a serious varietal.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Blended with Semillon in Margaret River and grown crisp in the Adelaide Hills; seldom the star it is across the Tasman.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.styles: The brown-skinned Muscat à Petits Grains, raisined on the vine and fortified in Rutherglen for the sweetest wine in the country.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: One of the Mediterranean varieties planted where the climate suits them, with Fiano, Vermentino and Nero d'Avola, especially in McLaren Vale.

exam: Place the five South Australian regions on the map and give each its one grape and one soil: Barossa Shiraz, Eden and Clare Riesling, McLaren Vale Grenache and Shiraz, Coonawarra Cabernet on terra rossa.
Know the GI ladder as origin only, zone to region to subregion, and the rule that a region must prove discreteness while a zone proves nothing.
Hold the 85 per cent rule for variety, vintage and region, the descending order of a blend's name, and the 95 per cent rule for a blend of up to three GIs.
Pair Grange, a multi-region South Australian Shiraz in American oak, against Hill of Grace, one Eden Valley vineyard from Henschke.
Explain Hunter Semillon's low-alcohol picking and bottle age, Rutherglen Muscat's raisining and fortification, and Tasmania's role as the sparkling base.
Name the retired European terms and what replaced them: Hermitage, Burgundy and Champagne first, then Sherry, Tokay and Port as Apera, Topaque and Tawny in 2010.
Say which states are phylloxera-free and why the oldest ungrafted Shiraz in the world is in South Australia.
traps: Barossa is a zone; Barossa Valley and Eden Valley are its two regions. A locator on the valley floor is not the whole zone.
Grange is a blend across South Australian regions; Hill of Grace is one vineyard in Eden Valley. Both are Shiraz-led, only one is a single site.
A label reading Cabernet Shiraz holds more Cabernet than Shiraz; the order is the proportion, never the winery's preference.
Australian Riesling is dry unless the label says otherwise; the German expectation of residual sugar is the wrong default.
Coonawarra is cool for Australia and its Cabernet is structured and minty, never jammy; terra rossa is red loam over limestone, not volcanic soil.
A Bin number is a Penfolds house code and Langton's is a private ranking; neither is law, and no GI carries a quality tier.
Hunter Semillon's toast comes from bottle age, not oak: the wine is picked at about 10 to 11 per cent alcohol and sees no barrel.

cards.f: Australian GI ladder: the three tiers from smallest to widest
cards.b: Subregion (the same size test, substantially discrete and homogeneous), region (one tract, five vineyards of five hectares, 500 tonnes, measurably discrete and homogeneous), zone (a grouping, no homogeneity). Origin only, no quality tier.

cards.f: The 85 per cent rule: which three claims it governs
cards.b: Variety, vintage and Geographical Indication: each stated claim must be at least 85 per cent of the wine, audited by the Label Integrity Programme since 1990.

cards.f: Reading a two-grape Australian label
cards.b: Descending order of proportion: Shiraz Cabernet holds more Shiraz. Named grapes together make 85 per cent and each named grape outweighs any unnamed one.

cards.f: Grange against Hill of Grace
cards.b: Grange: Penfolds, Shiraz blended across South Australian regions, new American oak, first made 1951. Hill of Grace: Henschke, one Eden Valley vineyard, Shiraz vines from the 1860s, first vintage 1958.

cards.f: Three phylloxera-free states to know
cards.b: South Australia, Western Australia and Tasmania. South Australia's border quarantine is why own-rooted Shiraz from the 1840s survives in the Barossa.

cards.f: South Eastern Australia: what the GI covers
cards.b: New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania whole, plus the grape-growing parts of Queensland and South Australia: the super-zone behind most blended export wine.

cards.f: Apera, Topaque, Tawny: the old names
cards.b: Sherry, Tokay and Port. Retired from Australian fortified labels in 2010 under the agreement with the European Union. Topaque is Muscadelle, not Furmint.

cards.f: Langton's Classification: what it is
cards.b: A private, auction-based ranking of Australia's collectible wines, revised periodically, in tiers of Exceptional, Outstanding and Excellent. Not a legal classification.

cards.f: The three hot inland districts and their rivers
cards.b: Riverland (Murray, South Australia), Murray Darling and Swan Hill (Murray, across Victoria and New South Wales), Riverina (Murrumbidgee, New South Wales). The bulk of everyday wine.

cards.f: The Barossa Old Vine Charter: four tiers and ages
cards.b: Old Vine 35 years, Survivor Vine 70, Centenarian Vine 100, Ancestor Vine 125. A regional charter of 2009, not national law.

questions.q: Which of these Geographical Indications is a zone rather than a region?
questions.exp: Barossa is the zone that holds the two regions Barossa Valley and Eden Valley; Clare Valley is a region of the neighbouring Mount Lofty Ranges zone.

questions.q: What minimum share of a wine must a single stated grape variety make up on an Australian label?
questions.exp: The Label Integrity Programme sets 85 per cent for a stated variety, vintage and Geographical Indication alike; a blend of named varieties must also total 85 per cent.

questions.q: Which grape leads the blend of Penfolds Grange?
questions.exp: Grange is Shiraz, sometimes with a small portion of Cabernet Sauvignon, blended across South Australian regions and matured in new American oak; it was first made in 1951.

questions.q: In which region does the Hill of Grace vineyard lie?
questions.exp: Hill of Grace is Henschke's single vineyard near Keyneton in Eden Valley, the higher, cooler region of the Barossa zone, with Shiraz vines planted in the 1860s.

questions.q: Which state has never had phylloxera and keeps a quarantine at its border to stay that way?
questions.exp: South Australia has never recorded phylloxera, which is why own-rooted vines from the 1840s survive in the Barossa; Western Australia and Tasmania are also free, while parts of Victoria and New South Wales are not.

questions.q: In what order are the grapes named on an Australian blend such as Shiraz Cabernet?
questions.exp: Named varieties are listed in descending order by volume, so Shiraz Cabernet holds more Shiraz than Cabernet; together the named grapes make at least 85 per cent of the wine.

questions.q: Which private classification ranks Australia's collectible wines as Exceptional, Outstanding and Excellent?
questions.exp: Langton's is an auction-house classification revised periodically from secondary-market demand; it carries no legal standing, because the GI system classifies origin only.

questions.q: Which grape variety is the most planted in Australia?
questions.exp: Shiraz is the most planted variety and the national red; Chardonnay is the most planted white and Cabernet Sauvignon the second red.

regions.name: Margaret River (WA)
regions.summary: Margaret River is the far south-western corner of Australia, a cape of granite and gravel between Cape Naturaliste and Cape Leeuwin, with the Indian Ocean to the west and north and the Southern Ocean to the south. The warm Leeuwin Current and constant sea breezes give it Australia's most even climate, which is why a 1965 study compared it to Bordeaux, whose Cabernet Sauvignon ripens here with a reliability Bordeaux can only envy. The first commercial vines went in at Vasse Felix in 1967. A server holds three wines: Cabernet Sauvignon with cedar, bay leaf and fine gravelly tannin; intense, stone-fruited Chardonnay from the Gingin clone; and the zesty unoaked Semillon Sauvignon Blanc blend the trade calls SSB.

terroir.climate: Maritime Mediterranean with the smallest swing between seasons of any Australian region. Winters are mild and wet, with around 1,100 millimetres of rain falling almost entirely between May and September; summers are warm, dry and breezy rather than hot. The Leeuwin Current, a warm flow running south along the coast, keeps winter frost away and spring even, so budburst and flowering are seldom disturbed. Vintage variation is low, which is the region's commercial strength.
terroir.soils: Gravelly, ironstone-flecked sandy loams over granite and gneiss of the Leeuwin-Naturaliste Ridge, free draining and low in fertility: the famous Forest Grove gravels. Nearer the coast the ancient rock gives way to limestone and dune sand, the limestone that holds the region's caves. Vines on the gravel carry moderate vigour and ripen Cabernet with fine, dusty tannin.
terroir.topography: A low ridge running roughly 100 kilometres north to south between the two capes and up to about 27 kilometres wide, the land gently rolling rather than steep, most vineyards between sea level and 100 metres among jarrah and marri forest. The ridge divides a thin coastal strip from the slightly warmer, more sheltered inland side.
terroir.water: The Indian Ocean on the west and Geographe Bay to the north supply the breezes and the Leeuwin Current the warmth. The Margaret River itself is a small stream that gives the town and the region their name; it matters less to the vines than the sea does.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The grape the region was planted for: blackcurrant, cedar, bay leaf and gravel dust, with fine firm tannin and medium alcohol, usually blended with a little Merlot, Malbec or Petit Verdot and built to age.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: From the Gingin clone, with its small, uneven berries, it gives concentrated white peach, grapefruit and nectarine with natural acidity; barrel fermented and often wild fermented, it is among Australia's longest-lived whites.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Blended with Semillon in the regional dry white, bright, herbal and citrus-led, mostly unoaked and drunk young.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: The other half of the SSB blend, lending weight, lemon and a grassy edge; a few houses barrel ferment it in the Graves manner.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Softens the Cabernet blends and appears alone from a handful of houses, plummy and medium-bodied.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: A cooler, spicier, red-fruited Shiraz than the South Australian norm, mid-weight and peppery.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: A traditional minor partner in the Cabernet blends, adding colour and plum.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.styles: A small seasoning in the Bordeaux-style blends, for colour, violet and tannin.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: A Western Australian staple from the Swan Valley, grown here in small amounts, fresh and appley, mostly in blends or as an everyday dry white.

grapes.name: Verdelho
grapes.styles: A Western Australian speciality inherited from the Swan Valley, tropical and dry, made as a summer white.

wines.note: Blackcurrant, cedar and bay leaf over fine gravelly tannin, medium to full in body at moderate alcohol, often with Merlot and Malbec in support. Decant a young one; it keeps for twenty years. Lamb with rosemary, beef with a red wine sauce.

Concentrated and long, white peach and grapefruit with a struck-match edge from barrel fermentation, acidity firm enough to age a decade. Serve cool rather than cold, with roasted chicken, crab or a cream sauce.
The region's everyday white, zesty, grassy and lime-fresh, usually unoaked and bottled under screwcap for drinking within two years. Oysters, ceviche and goat's cheese.
A softer Bordeaux-style blend for the table, red and black fruit with a leafy edge and gentle tannin; the house red of the region.
Cooler and spicier than Barossa, red cherry and white pepper with medium body; a reminder that the region's maritime air suits grapes beyond Cabernet.

made.viticulture: Vines are trained on vertical shoot positioning and picked by machine or hand between February for Chardonnay and April for Cabernet, under a sky that rarely rains during harvest. Disease pressure is low and rot is rare, so the hazards are the wind, which can scorch exposed canopies and reduce fruit set, and the birds: silvereyes strip ripening grapes, and growers watch the marri trees, because when the marri blossoms heavily the birds feed there instead and the nets can stay rolled. Dry-grown vines are possible on deeper soils, but most blocks carry drip irrigation for the rainless summer. The Gingin clone of Chardonnay, brought into Western Australia through the Gingin research station in the 1950s, sets uneven bunches of large and tiny berries, the hen-and-chicken pattern, which cuts yield and concentrates flavour; it is the clone the region's reputation rests on. Cabernet sites on the gravel inland are warmer and more sheltered than the coastal strip. The region's six districts, Yallingup, Carbunup, Wilyabrup, Treeton, Wallcliffe and Karridale, were drawn in a 1999 study and remain unofficial; Wilyabrup's own application for a subregion GI won an interim determination in December 2019, but the committee made no final determination in August 2020, so it remains unregistered.
made.winemaking: Cabernet is made in the Bordeaux manner: cool fermentation in open or closed tanks, gentle extraction, a year to eighteen months in French barriques with a measured share of new oak, and blending with Merlot, Malbec or Petit Verdot before bottling; the aim is structure and perfume, not weight. Chardonnay is whole-bunch pressed to barrel, fermented often with wild yeasts, kept on lees with some stirring, and the malolactic conversion is partly or wholly blocked to keep the acid line; the struck-match reductive note is a regional signature. The SSB blend is cold fermented in stainless steel, sometimes with a barrel-fermented portion of Semillon, and bottled early under screwcap. Alcohol is moderate across the board because the sea air ripens flavour before sugar runs away. A few houses farm biodynamically, and the region as a whole bottles a high share of its wine as estate-grown rather than bought fruit.

law.classification: Margaret River is a registered region of the Western Australian South West Australia zone, one of the earliest regions entered on the national register in the 1990s. The GI fixes a boundary and nothing more: no grape, yield or style is written into law, and the 85 per cent rule for variety, vintage and origin applies as everywhere in Australia. There are no registered subregions; the six districts are a vigneron's map, not a legal one, though Wilyabrup was pursued as a subregion from 2017 until the committee declined to finalise it in August 2020. Quality signals are the house and the vineyard, and Langton's lists several of the region's Cabernets and Chardonnays, privately.
tiers: Zone: South West Australia
The wide zone that holds Margaret River, Great Southern, Pemberton, Manjimup, Geographe and Blackwood Valley; a grouping with no homogeneity required.
Region: Margaret River
The registered GI from Cape Naturaliste to Cape Leeuwin, the whole of the cape; 85 per cent of a wine so labelled must come from inside the line.
Districts (unofficial)

Yallingup, Carbunup, Wilyabrup, Treeton, Wallcliffe and Karridale, drawn in a 1999 climate study and used by growers; Wilyabrup's registration as a subregion won an interim determination in December 2019, but no final determination followed in August 2020, so none is registered.
labels: SSB or SBS
Semillon Sauvignon Blanc or Sauvignon Blanc Semillon: the first grape is the larger share, by the national descending order rule.
Art Series
Leeuwin Estate's top tier, named for the commissioned paintings on its labels; a house term, not law.
Estate
Unregulated in law, but the region's leading houses grow most of their own fruit.

places.name: Wilyabrup
places.note: The heartland in the north-centre of the region, on gravelly loam over granite, where the pioneering vineyards of the late 1960s and 1970s were planted and where the most structured Cabernet grows. The district applied for its own GI in 2017; the application was not finalised in 2020 and it remains unregistered.

places.name: Cowaramup
places.note: The hamlet in Wilyabrup's heart, around which several of the founding estates stand; the name a server meets on labels and directions, not a GI.

places.name: Yallingup
places.note: The northern tip near Cape Naturaliste, exposed to the sea wind, with early-ripening Cabernet and Chardonnay on gravel and limestone.

places.name: Carbunup
places.note: The north-eastern inland district towards Geographe Bay, flatter, warmer and more sheltered from the sea wind; a source of generous reds and the region's everyday whites.

places.name: Treeton
places.note: The forested inland centre, east of Wilyabrup and sheltered from the sea wind, with later-ripening fruit and a cooler night; mixed plantings of Chardonnay and Cabernet.

places.name: Wallcliffe
places.note: The centre-west around the town of Margaret River and the river mouth, where limestone and sand meet gravel; the home of the Chardonnay that made the region's name and of balanced Cabernet.

places.name: Karridale
places.note: The southern end towards Cape Leeuwin, the coolest and wettest district, named for the karri forest; later harvests, bright Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon and Chardonnay, and leaner Cabernet.

places.name: Western Australia beyond the cape
places.note: The rest of the state's wine lies in the South West Australia zone and the Swan District north of Perth; a server meets these names on lists of Riesling, Shiraz and Verdelho.

places.name: Great Southern
places.note: The vast cool region on the south coast, with five subregions: Frankland River and Mount Barker for Riesling, Shiraz and Cabernet, Porongurup for Riesling on granite, Denmark and Albany for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay near the sea.

places.name: Pemberton and Manjimup
places.note: Inland karri-forest regions south-east of Margaret River, cooler and wetter, growing Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc.

places.name: Geographe
places.note: The coastal region north-east of Margaret River around Bunbury, warmer, with Shiraz, Cabernet and Mediterranean varieties.

places.name: Swan Valley
places.note: The historic hot region just north of Perth, planted in the 1830s, the home of Western Australian Verdelho, Chenin Blanc and fortified wine; a subregion of the Swan District.

producers.name: Vasse Felix
producers.why: The region's first commercial vineyard, planted in 1967 by a Perth doctor whose faith in the cape's Cabernet proved right.

producers.name: Moss Wood
producers.why: Planted in Wilyabrup in 1969, its Cabernet Sauvignon is the region's most classical and most collected.

producers.name: Cullen Wines
producers.why: Founded in 1971 and farmed biodynamically, famous for a Cabernet-Merlot blend and a long-lived Chardonnay.

producers.name: Leeuwin Estate
producers.why: Planted in 1974 on a Napa legend's advice; its Art Series Chardonnay is the wine that put Australian Chardonnay among the world's best.

producers.name: Cape Mentelle
producers.why: Founded in 1970, it won Australia's Jimmy Watson Trophy in 1983 and 1984 with its Cabernet, and its founder went on to start Cloudy Bay in Marlborough.

producers.name: Woodlands
producers.why: A Wilyabrup estate from 1973 whose Cabernet is quietly among the region's finest.

producers.name: Pierro
producers.why: A benchmark for rich, barrel-fermented Chardonnay and a serious Cabernet blend.

producers.name: Voyager Estate
producers.why: A large Wallcliffe estate known for Chardonnay and Cabernet of consistent polish and its Cape Dutch architecture.

exam: Place the region at the south-western corner of the continent, between Cape Naturaliste and Cape Leeuwin, and name the Indian Ocean and the Leeuwin Current as its climate.
Give the two lead grapes, Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay, and the Semillon Sauvignon Blanc blend as the third wine.
Explain why the climate is compared to Bordeaux: maritime, even, with winter rain and a dry, reliable harvest.
Know the soil as gravelly loam over granite and gneiss, and the Gingin clone as the reason the Chardonnay is concentrated.
Name Vasse Felix as the first commercial vineyard of 1967, and Leeuwin Estate's Art Series as the famous Chardonnay.
At Advanced, list the six unofficial districts and know that Wilyabrup is the Cabernet heartland.
traps: Margaret River is maritime and even, not hot: its Cabernet is medium-bodied and cedary, nearer Bordeaux than Barossa.
The Leeuwin Current is a warm current, not a cold one; it moderates winter and spring rather than chilling the summer.
The six districts are unofficial; only Margaret River itself is a registered GI, within the South West Australia zone.
SSB and SBS are the same blend with the proportions reversed; the first grape named is the larger share.
The region's Chardonnay clone is Gingin, after a Western Australian town, not a French clone; some books call it the Mendoza clone.
The Margaret River itself is a small stream; the region's water is the ocean on three sides.

cards.b: Cape Naturaliste in the north and Cape Leeuwin in the south, about 100 kilometres apart; the Indian Ocean on the west and Geographe Bay to the north.

cards.f: Margaret River: the current and what it does
cards.b: The Leeuwin Current, a warm flow running south along the coast, keeps winters mild and springs frost-free, giving the most even climate in Australia.

cards.f: Margaret River: the two lead grapes and the third wine
cards.b: Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay lead; the Semillon Sauvignon Blanc blend, SSB, is the everyday white.

cards.f: Margaret River: the soil in one line
cards.b: Gravelly, ironstone-flecked sandy loam over granite and gneiss (the Forest Grove gravels); limestone and sand nearer the coast.

cards.f: The Gingin clone: what it is and why it matters
cards.b: Margaret River's Chardonnay clone, brought in through the Gingin research station in the 1950s; its hen-and-chicken bunches cut yield and concentrate flavour.

cards.f: Margaret River: first commercial vineyard and year
cards.b: Vasse Felix, planted in 1967 in Wilyabrup by a Perth doctor; Moss Wood followed in 1969, Cape Mentelle in 1970, Cullen in 1971, Leeuwin Estate in 1974.

cards.f: Margaret River's six unofficial districts
cards.b: Yallingup, Carbunup, Wilyabrup, Treeton, Wallcliffe, Karridale, north to south, drawn in a 1999 study; Wilyabrup is the Cabernet heartland.

cards.f: Which Marlborough house did a Margaret River founder start
cards.b: Cloudy Bay, founded in 1985 by the founder of Cape Mentelle, who had just won two Jimmy Watson Trophies with Margaret River Cabernet.

questions.q: Which ocean current moderates the climate of Margaret River?
questions.exp: The warm Leeuwin Current runs south along the Western Australian coast and keeps Margaret River's winters mild and its springs even; the Humboldt and Benguela currents are cold flows off Chile and South Africa.

questions.q: To which French region is Margaret River's climate most often compared?
questions.exp: A 1965 study matched the cape's maritime, even climate to Bordeaux, which is why Cabernet Sauvignon was the grape planted first and still leads.

questions.q: Which clone of Chardonnay, with its hen-and-chicken bunches, gives Margaret River its concentrated whites?
questions.exp: The Gingin clone came into Western Australia through the Gingin research station in the 1950s; its uneven berry set lowers yield and concentrates flavour, and some references call it the Mendoza clone.

questions.q: Which unofficial district is regarded as the heartland of Margaret River Cabernet Sauvignon?
questions.exp: Wilyabrup, in the north-centre on gravel over granite, holds the founding vineyards and the most structured Cabernet; Karridale in the south is the coolest district and Yallingup the exposed northern tip.

questions.q: Which estate planted Margaret River's first commercial vineyard in 1967?
questions.exp: Vasse Felix was planted in 1967 by a Perth doctor acting on the 1965 climate study; Moss Wood, Cape Mentelle, Cullen and Leeuwin Estate followed within seven years.

questions.q: Which two grapes make Margaret River's classic dry white blend?
questions.exp: The Semillon Sauvignon Blanc blend, labelled SSB or SBS by proportion, is the region's zesty everyday white, mostly unoaked and drunk young.

questions.q: In which zone of Western Australia does the Margaret River region lie?
questions.exp: Margaret River is a region of the South West Australia zone with Great Southern, Pemberton, Manjimup, Geographe and Blackwood Valley; Greater Perth holds the Swan District, Perth Hills and Peel, and the other two zones hold almost no vines.

questions.q: Which Margaret River estate makes the Art Series Chardonnay?
questions.exp: Leeuwin Estate was planted in 1974 on a Napa vintner's advice; its Art Series Chardonnay, named for the commissioned paintings on its labels, put Australian Chardonnay among the world's best and is the region's most famous white.

regions.name: Barossa / Eden Valley (SA)
regions.summary: Barossa is a zone an hour north-east of Adelaide that holds two registered regions: the warm Barossa Valley on the floor, and the higher, cooler Eden Valley in the ranges to its east, with High Eden as a subregion. Silesian Lutherans and English settlers planted it from 1842, South Australia has never had phylloxera, and so Shiraz on its own roots from the 1840s still crops here. The valley floor makes Australia's most famous red, ripe, chocolatey Shiraz, with old bush-vine Grenache and Mataro beside it; Eden Valley makes bone-dry, lime-scented Riesling and finer, more perfumed Shiraz, including Henschke's Hill of Grace. Grange, Penfolds' multi-region Shiraz, is the Barossa's other flagship, and the exam asks the pair every time.

terroir.climate: The Barossa Valley is warm and Mediterranean, with hot dry summers, around 500 millimetres of winter rain, and enough sunshine to ripen Shiraz to full flesh; afternoon heat is tempered a little by gully winds and by cool nights. Eden Valley, 200 to 300 metres higher in the Barossa Ranges, is distinctly cooler and windier, with rain nearer 700 millimetres, a later budburst and a harvest two to three weeks behind the floor, which is why it keeps acid in Riesling and perfume in Shiraz.
terroir.soils: The valley floor is a patchwork rather than one soil: red-brown earths and clay loams, grey-brown sandy loams over clay, pockets of ironstone and limestone, deeper sands in the north around Ebenezer and Kalimna. Eden Valley sits on the old rock of the ranges: shallow, acidic, gravelly loams over weathered schist and gneiss with quartz, poor and free draining, which holds yields down.
terroir.topography: The Barossa Valley floor runs north-east to south-west between about 230 and 400 metres, from Lyndoch and Williamstown in the south through Tanunda and Nuriootpa to Greenock, Ebenezer and Kalimna in the north, with the Western Ridge rising on one side and the Barossa Ranges on the other. Eden Valley is the hill country of those ranges between about 380 and 600 metres, around Angaston's hinterland, Keyneton, Springton and Eden Valley township, with High Eden its highest southern reach.
terroir.water: The North Para River threads the valley floor from Nuriootpa down through Tanunda and Lyndoch; it is a seasonal stream, not a climate moderator. Water for irrigation is drawn from bores and the regional scheme; old dry-grown bush vines on the floor manage without.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The Barossa's grape in both regions: on the floor rich, dark, plum and chocolate with liquorice and sweet oak, full-bodied and high in alcohol; in Eden Valley more perfumed, peppery and medium to full, with firmer acid.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Eden Valley's white: bone dry, lime, white flowers and talc with steely acid at 11 to 12.5 per cent alcohol, under screwcap, ageing into toast and honey over a decade.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: Old bush vines on the sandy floor, once picked for fortified wine, now a perfumed, raspberry-scented mid-weight red and the G of the Barossa GSM blend.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.styles: Called Mataro here, from vines as old as any: dark, meaty, earthy and tannic, the M of GSM and occasionally a varietal from a single ancient block.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Blended with Shiraz in the South Australian manner, as in Penfolds Bin 389 and Yalumba's The Signature, and grown alone on cooler Eden Valley slopes.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: The historic Barossa white, once oaked and rich; the modern style is fresher and lemony from old vines on the floor.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Grown mostly in Eden Valley's cooler air for a mid-weight, citrus and stone fruit white.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: A Yalumba speciality in Eden Valley, apricot-scented and full, and a small co-ferment partner for Shiraz.

wines.note: Full-bodied, warm and plush: blackberry, plum, dark chocolate and liquorice, with sweet vanilla from American oak in the traditional houses and more cedar from French oak in others. Decant, serve just below room temperature, and give it a braised short rib or a char-grilled steak.

Bone dry and taut, lime, lemon blossom and talc with a slatey finish; it tastes of citrus at two years and of toast and honey at ten. Serve cold with oysters, Thai or Vietnamese dishes, or a crab salad.
Finer and more perfumed than the floor: red and black fruit, pepper, dried herbs and firmer acid at medium to full body; Hill of Grace and Mount Edelstone are the names.
Grenache, Shiraz and Mataro from old bush vines, the Barossa's answer to the southern Rhône: raspberry, spice and earth, medium to full, friendly young. Roast pork, lamb shoulder, sausages.

Shiraz from several South Australian regions with the Barossa at its heart, matured in new American oak and released four or five years after vintage; dense, mocha-rich and built for decades. The country's most famous red.

The Barossa's fortified heritage: a barrel of tawny laid down every year since 1878 and released at a hundred years old, with younger blends beside it; toffee, walnut and rancio, served in small pours with hard cheese or alone.

made.viticulture: The valley floor still carries bush vines on their own roots, some planted in the 1840s, because phylloxera never reached South Australia and the state polices its border to keep it so; the Barossa Old Vine Charter of 2009 names them Old at 35 years, Survivor at 70, Centenarian at 100 and Ancestor at 125. Younger blocks are trellised, drip irrigated and machine harvested; the oldest are dry grown and hand picked. Heat and drought are the hazards on the floor, where a hot spell can shrivel Shiraz and lift sugar ahead of flavour, so picking date is the great decision. Eden Valley's rocky, thin soils and wind keep yields low, and its later season lets Riesling hang for flavour while holding acid; spring frost and poor set in cold windy years are its risks. The Barossa Grounds project maps the floor into unofficial grounds, northern, central and southern with the eastern edge and western ridge, which growers use to explain why Ebenezer's sand and Lyndoch's clay give different Shiraz.
made.winemaking: Shiraz is fermented in open vats, often with headboards and pump-overs rather than hard plunging, and the traditional houses still press in slow basket presses. Maturation is in hogsheads and puncheons; American oak gave the classic Barossa vanilla and coconut, and Penfolds built Grange on it, while many houses now lean on French oak for cedar and finer grain. Alcohol commonly sits around 14.5 per cent and the best makers manage it by picking earlier, adding whole bunches and shortening the time in new barrels. Grange is blended across regions and matured about eighteen months in new American oak hogsheads; Bin 389 matures in the barrels that held the previous Grange, which earned it the name Baby Grange. GSM blends are built from separate old-vine parcels and kept in older wood. Eden Valley Riesling is picked early, pressed gently, fermented cool in stainless steel to dryness and bottled under screwcap within months, with no oak and no malolactic conversion. The fortified tradition survives in Seppeltsfield's solera-like tawny cellars and in a few houses' vintage fortified Shiraz.

law.classification: Barossa is a registered zone, and inside it Barossa Valley and Eden Valley are two registered regions with distinct boundaries; High Eden is a registered subregion in the south of Eden Valley. A wine labelled Barossa may blend both regions; a wine labelled Barossa Valley must take 85 per cent from the floor. No law writes grapes, yields or ageing into any of these lines. The Old Vine Charter is a voluntary regional code, and Bin numbers and Langton's standings are house codes and a private ranking. A wine labelled South Australia, such as Grange, is a state-level GI blend that need not say which regions it draws on.
tiers: Zone: Barossa
The zone of the two valleys; a blend of floor and hills fruit is labelled Barossa.
Region: Barossa Valley
The warm floor north-east of Adelaide, from Lyndoch to Kalimna: 85 per cent of the wine from inside the line.
Region: Eden Valley
The higher, cooler hill country of the Barossa Ranges to the east, registered separately; Riesling and perfumed Shiraz.
Subregion: High Eden
The highest, southern part of Eden Valley, the only registered subregion in the zone.
Old Vine Charter
A voluntary Barossa code of 2009: Old Vine 35 years, Survivor 70, Centenarian 100, Ancestor 125; not national law.
labels: Barossa
A zone blend that may mix Barossa Valley and Eden Valley fruit.
Bin 389
A Penfolds house code for its Cabernet Shiraz, matured in ex-Grange barrels; the name order means more Cabernet than Shiraz.
Ancestor Vine
A charter term for a vine of 125 years or more; not a legal claim.
Hermitage
The French name Grange carried as Grange Hermitage until about 1990, retired under the agreement with Europe.

places.name: Barossa Valley
places.note: The warm floor and the heart of Australian Shiraz, settled by Silesian Lutherans from 1842 and planted at Jacob's Creek in 1847; the villages of Tanunda, Nuriootpa, Angaston, Lyndoch and Greenock still carry the German churches and bakeries.

places.name: Northern Grounds
places.note: The warmest, driest reach around Ebenezer, Kalimna, Moppa and Greenock on deep sands and red earth, giving the densest, most opulent Shiraz.

places.name: Central Grounds
places.note: The floor around Tanunda, Nuriootpa, Marananga, Seppeltsfield and Stonewell, the historic core, with clay loams and the oldest vineyards.

places.name: Southern Grounds
places.note: The cooler, wetter south around Lyndoch, Rowland Flat and Williamstown, on heavier clay soils, giving a slightly finer, fresher Shiraz.

places.name: Marananga
places.note: A village on the western side of the central floor, home of Torbreck and a source of plush, chocolatey Shiraz from old vines.

places.name: Seppeltsfield
places.note: The village built around the Seppelt family's 1851 winery, with its palm-lined avenue and the cellars that hold the Para tawny laid down every year since 1878.

places.name: Eden Valley
places.note: The cool hill country east of the floor, its first vines planted at Pewsey Vale in 1847, registered as its own region: Riesling of lime and slate, and Shiraz of perfume and pepper from vineyards such as Hill of Grace and Mount Edelstone near Keyneton.

places.name: High Eden
places.note: The highest and coolest part of Eden Valley at its southern end, a registered subregion, with the finest Riesling and Chardonnay.

places.name: Keyneton
places.note: The hamlet where the Henschke family has made wine since 1868; Hill of Grace, planted in the 1860s and first bottled alone in 1958, and Mount Edelstone, planted in 1912, lie nearby.

places.name: Pewsey Vale
places.note: Eden Valley's first vineyard, planted in 1847 and replanted to Riesling in 1961 by Yalumba; a benchmark for the dry, ageworthy style.

places.name: Angaston
places.note: The town at the foot of the ranges where Yalumba was founded in 1849; it sits on the seam between the two regions.

producers.name: Penfolds
producers.why: Founded at Magill in 1844; Grange, first made in 1951, and the Bin series made South Australian Shiraz and Cabernet Shiraz famous across the world.

producers.name: Henschke
producers.why: Making wine at Keyneton since 1868; Hill of Grace is the single-vineyard Eden Valley Shiraz the exam sets against Grange, and its Rieslings are benchmarks too.

producers.name: Yalumba
producers.why: Founded at Angaston in 1849, Australia's oldest family-owned winery, with Pewsey Vale Riesling, The Signature Cabernet Shiraz and a long devotion to Viognier.

producers.name: Seppeltsfield
producers.why: The 1851 estate whose cellars hold a barrel of tawny from every vintage since 1878, released at one hundred years old.

producers.name: Torbreck Vintners
producers.why: Founded at Marananga in 1994 and built on old-vine Shiraz, Grenache and Mataro in a lavish Rhône-inspired style.

producers.name: Rockford
producers.why: A Krondorf house of 1984 that kept the basket press and the open vat; its Basket Press Shiraz is the traditionalist's Barossa.

producers.name: Peter Lehmann Wines
producers.why: Founded in 1979 to buy the grapes of growers the big companies had dropped, and now a house of honest Barossa Shiraz, Semillon and Eden Valley Riesling.

producers.name: St Hallett
producers.why: A valley-floor house whose Old Block Shiraz, from very old vines, is one of the region's reference wines.

producers.name: Jacob's Creek
producers.why: The brand that took Barossa's name to every supermarket in the world, named for the creek where the valley's first commercial vines were planted in 1847.

exam: Separate the zone from its two regions: Barossa holds Barossa Valley and Eden Valley, and High Eden is the subregion.
Give the floor its grape and style, Shiraz, rich and chocolatey from old own-rooted vines, and the hills theirs, dry Riesling and perfumed Shiraz.
Know Grange against Hill of Grace: Penfolds' multi-region South Australian Shiraz in American oak, against Henschke's single Eden Valley vineyard.
Hold the Old Vine Charter tiers and years, and why phylloxera's absence lets 1840s vines survive.
Name the GSM blend's three grapes and why Grenache and Mataro are in the Barossa at all.
At Advanced, know the Barossa Grounds, Pewsey Vale's 1847 and 1961 dates, Mount Edelstone and Bin 389's ex-Grange barrels.
traps: Barossa the zone, Barossa Valley the region: a Barossa label may mix in Eden Valley fruit, a Barossa Valley label may not.
Eden Valley is in the Barossa zone; Clare Valley is not, it belongs to the Mount Lofty Ranges zone further north.
Grange carries a South Australia GI, not Barossa, because it blends regions; Hill of Grace is one Eden Valley vineyard.
Mataro is Mourvèdre, not a separate grape; the M of GSM is the same vine as Bandol's.
Old Vine is unregulated nationally; the Barossa charter's tiers are voluntary and begin at 35 years, not 50.
Grange is matured in American oak, not French; many modern Barossa houses now prefer French, but the flagship never changed.
Eden Valley Riesling is dry; its toast and honey at ten years come from age, not sweetness or oak.

cards.f: Eden Valley: its two wines
cards.b: Bone-dry Riesling of lime, flowers and slate under screwcap, and perfumed, peppery Shiraz with firmer acid, from vineyards such as Hill of Grace and Mount Edelstone.

cards.f: Grange: house, grape, oak, origin
cards.b: Penfolds; Shiraz with sometimes a little Cabernet; new American oak hogsheads for about eighteen months; a blend across South Australian regions, first made in 1951, labelled Grange Hermitage until about 1990.

cards.f: The Barossa Old Vine Charter tiers
cards.b: Old Vine 35 years, Survivor Vine 70, Centenarian Vine 100, Ancestor Vine 125; a voluntary regional charter of 2009.

cards.f: GSM: the three grapes and the model
cards.b: Grenache, Shiraz and Mataro (Mourvèdre), from old bush vines, in the manner of the southern Rhône's Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre.

cards.f: Why 1840s vines survive in the Barossa
cards.b: South Australia has never had phylloxera and quarantines its border, so vines on their own roots planted by the first settlers still crop.

cards.f: Barossa founding dates to know
cards.b: Settlement 1842; Jacob's Creek vines 1847; Pewsey Vale 1847; Yalumba 1849; Seppeltsfield 1851; Henschke at Keyneton 1868; Penfolds at Magill, Adelaide, 1844.

cards.b: Penfolds' Cabernet Shiraz, more Cabernet than Shiraz by the name order, matured in the American oak barrels that held the previous vintage's Grange.

questions.q: Which zone holds both the Barossa Valley and Eden Valley regions?
questions.exp: Barossa is the zone and the two valleys are its registered regions; Mount Lofty Ranges holds Clare Valley and the Adelaide Hills, Fleurieu holds McLaren Vale and Limestone Coast holds Coonawarra.

questions.q: To which grape is the Hill of Grace vineyard planted?
questions.exp: Hill of Grace is Henschke's single-vineyard Eden Valley Shiraz, from vines planted in the 1860s and first bottled alone in 1958; the house also makes Riesling, but not from that site.

questions.q: At what age does a vine qualify as an Ancestor Vine under the Barossa Old Vine Charter?
questions.exp: The 2009 charter sets Old Vine at 35 years, Survivor at 70, Centenarian at 100 and Ancestor at 125; it is a voluntary regional code, not national law.

questions.q: Which white grape is Eden Valley's signature?
questions.exp: Eden Valley's height and wind keep acid in Riesling, giving the dry lime-and-slate style; Semillon is the old Barossa floor white and Viognier a Yalumba speciality.

questions.q: Which house, founded at Angaston in 1849, is Australia's oldest family-owned winery?
questions.exp: Yalumba was founded by an English brewer at Angaston in 1849 and remains in the same family; Seppeltsfield dates from 1851, Penfolds from 1844 at Magill and Henschke from 1868.

questions.q: Which subregion is registered within Eden Valley?
questions.exp: High Eden is the highest, coolest southern part of Eden Valley and the only registered subregion in the Barossa zone; the Barossa Grounds on the floor are unofficial.

questions.q: Which French name did Penfolds Grange carry on its label until about 1990?
questions.exp: The wine was sold as Grange Hermitage, Hermitage being the old Australian word for Shiraz, until the name was retired under the agreement with Europe; the other three are northern Rhône appellations never borrowed.

questions.q: In which kind of oak is Penfolds Grange matured?
questions.exp: Grange matures for about eighteen months in new American oak hogsheads, the source of its mocha and vanilla; Bin 389 then uses the same barrels, earning the name Baby Grange.

regions.name: Clare Valley (SA)
regions.summary: Clare Valley is a string of narrow valleys about 130 kilometres north of Adelaide, in the Mount Lofty Ranges zone, not the Barossa, standing 400 to 500 metres up where hot days give way to cold nights. It is Australia's Riesling capital: bone dry, lime and slate, high in acid, bottled under screwcap since the Riesling makers switched together for the 2000 vintage. Watervale gives the floral, limey style and Polish Hill River the flintier, slower one. The reds are serious too: firm, minty Shiraz and the old Clare pairing of Cabernet Sauvignon with Malbec. The Jesuits founded Sevenhill in 1851, the oldest winery in the valley, and the vines have never seen phylloxera.

terroir.climate: Continental for South Australia: warm to hot summer days, dry air and around 600 millimetres of mostly winter rain, but with cold nights that follow the elevation, and afternoon winds that reach up from the gulfs to the south-west. The wide swing between day and night is what keeps acid in Riesling picked in late February and March. Harvest for the reds runs into April, and spring frost on the valley floors is the main climatic risk.
terroir.soils: Varied along the valleys and the reason the sub-districts taste different. Watervale has red loam over limestone, a terra rossa of its own, with shale; Polish Hill River has hard, thin, slatey shale over clay, infertile and slow; around Clare and Sevenhill the soils are red-brown earths and stony loams. The slate of Polish Hill is the TERROIR row's clue to the whole valley.
terroir.topography: A north-south run of ridges and valleys about 40 kilometres long, from Auburn in the south through Watervale, Penwortham and Sevenhill to Clare in the north, with the Polish Hill River valley to the east and the Armagh and Skilly hills to the west, most vineyards between about 400 and 550 metres. The relief creates many small aspects, so a single hillside can hold two microclimates.
terroir.water: There is no large river. The Wakefield and Hutt rivers rise here as small seasonal streams, and vineyards rely on winter rain, stored dam water and bores; irrigation is restrained and many old vineyards are dry grown.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: The valley's identity: dry, lime juice and lemon zest, talc and slate, searing acid at 11.5 to 13 per cent alcohol, under screwcap, turning to toast, honey and a petrol-like note over ten to twenty years.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Full-bodied and firm with blackberry, mint and eucalypt, more structured and less plush than Barossa; The Armagh is the famous one.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Blackcurrant and mint with firm tannin, often blended with Malbec in the old Clare manner, as at Wendouree and Jim Barry.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: A Clare tradition since the nineteenth century, adding plum and softness to Cabernet and occasionally bottled alone.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: Old bush vines on the warmer slopes, giving spicy, medium-weight reds and blends.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: A small, old-vine white tradition, lemony and sometimes lightly oaked, and a partner for Riesling in a few blends.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: A secondary white from cooler sites, mid-weight and citrus-led.

wines.note: Bone dry and electric: fresh lime, lemon, white flowers and wet slate, with acid that makes the mouth water and a long clean finish. Serve cold with raw oysters, Vietnamese herbs, spicy Thai dishes or grilled fish; cellar ten years and it turns to toast and honey.
The softer, more floral face of Clare from red loam over limestone: lime blossom, orange peel and a rounder middle, approachable young.
The austere face from slate and shale: tighter, flintier, more mineral, lower in fruit when young and slower to unfold; the one to cellar.
Full and firm, blackberry, mint and eucalypt with chewy tannin and some French or American oak; built to age. Roast lamb, steak, braised oxtail.
The old Clare blend: blackcurrant and plum, mint and leather, dense and long-lived, from houses that have made it for a century.

A Clare sweet speciality: the canes are cut and the fruit left to raisin on the vine, giving lime marmalade and honey with Riesling's acid intact; Mount Horrocks made the style famous. A small pour with fruit tart or blue cheese.

made.viticulture: Vines sit between about 400 and 550 metres on slopes that face every direction, so site selection is the first decision: Riesling on cooler, slatier or limestone slopes, Shiraz and Cabernet on warmer red earth. Rainfall is modest and summer is dry, so most vineyards carry drip irrigation drawn from dams and bores, though many old blocks, including some planted in the 1890s, are dry grown. Training is mostly vertical shoot positioning, with old bush vines among the Grenache and Shiraz; harvest is by hand on the steep and old sites and by machine on the flat. Riesling is picked early for acid, often in late February, at modest sugar; the reds hang into April. Frost in low pockets, drought and the occasional heatwave are the hazards, and disease pressure is low in the dry air. Phylloxera has never arrived, and the valley's vignerons were the first in Australia to act together on closures: for the 2000 vintage thirteen Riesling producers bottled under screwcap to end cork taint and random oxidation, and the rest of the country followed within a few years.
made.winemaking: Riesling is made to show the vineyard and nothing else: whole-bunch pressing, settled juice, a cool fermentation in stainless steel to complete dryness, no oak, no malolactic conversion, no lees stirring, and bottling under screwcap within a few months of vintage. Alcohol lands between 11.5 and 13 per cent and residual sugar is close to nil, which is why the German expectation of sweetness is the wrong default. A few houses make an off-dry or a late-harvest Riesling and say so on the label. The reds are made traditionally: open fermentation, moderate extraction, pressing in basket presses at the old houses, and maturation in a mix of French and American oak hogsheads for twelve to twenty-four months. Cabernet and Malbec are often co-fermented or blended before barrel, a habit that goes back to the nineteenth century. The result is firm, age-worthy wine that softens over a decade rather than impressing in its first year.

law.classification: Clare Valley is a registered region of the Mount Lofty Ranges zone, which it shares with the Adelaide Hills and the Adelaide Plains; it is not in the Barossa zone, whatever its nearness on a map suggests. The GI draws the boundary and nothing more, and the 85 per cent rule for variety, vintage and origin applies. The sub-districts, Auburn, Watervale, Penwortham, Sevenhill, Polish Hill River, Clare and Armagh, are not registered subregions, though Watervale and Polish Hill River appear on labels as vineyard or district names under the house's word. Screwcap closure is a regional habit, not a legal rule.
tiers: Zone: Mount Lofty Ranges
Clare Valley, Adelaide Hills and Adelaide Plains; a zone with no homogeneity requirement.
Region: Clare Valley
The registered GI covering the valleys from Auburn to Clare; 85 per cent of a Clare Valley wine comes from inside the line.
Sub-districts (unofficial)
Auburn, Watervale, Penwortham, Sevenhill, Polish Hill River, Clare, Armagh: growers' names with no registered status, Watervale and Polish Hill River being the two a server will see on labels.
labels: Polish Hill
A vineyard name on Grosset's Riesling from the Polish Hill River district; a house term tied to a real place.
Springvale
Grosset's Watervale Riesling, named for its vineyard; a house term.
The Armagh
Jim Barry's flagship Shiraz, named for the Armagh hamlet west of Clare; a house term.

places.name: Watervale
places.note: The southern-central district on red loam over limestone with shale: the floral, limey, rounder Riesling, and the Florita vineyard planted in 1962 that Jim Barry bought in 1986.

places.name: Polish Hill River
places.note: A side valley to the east named for Polish settlers, with hard slatey shale over clay: austere, flinty, slow-ageing Riesling, the yardstick of which is Grosset's Polish Hill.

places.name: Sevenhill
places.note: The district around the Jesuit winery of 1851, the oldest in the valley and still making sacramental wine, and the home of Wendouree, founded in 1895 and the source of the valley's most uncompromising reds.

places.name: Auburn
places.note: The southern gateway, slightly warmer and lower, where Grosset has made Riesling since 1981.

places.name: Clare and Armagh
places.note: The northern town that names the region, with the Armagh hamlet to its west where Jim Barry's flagship Shiraz is grown; red-brown earths and a warmer, fuller style.

places.name: Penwortham
places.note: Between Watervale and Sevenhill, the site of the valley's first vines in 1840, planted by John Horrocks, the English pioneer who died in 1846 and whose name a Watervale house and the hill above the valley still carry.

places.name: The Mount Lofty Ranges zone beyond Clare
places.note: The zone's two other regions sit close to Adelaide rather than Clare; a server meets both on lists.

places.name: Adelaide Hills
places.note: The cool, wet hill country directly above Adelaide, high in the ranges, with Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and sparkling wine, and the subregions of Piccadilly Valley and Lenswood; cooler than Clare and far wetter.

places.name: Piccadilly Valley
places.note: The registered subregion nearest Adelaide, the coolest, for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and sparkling base.

places.name: Lenswood
places.note: The registered subregion to the north-east, high and steep, for Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Adelaide Plains
places.note: The flat, hot country north of the city, a source of ripe Shiraz and Grenache and of the vineyards that fed the big companies.

producers.name: Grosset
producers.why: Founded at Auburn in 1981; its Polish Hill and Springvale Rieslings are the two reference wines of Clare and the pair every student tastes side by side.

producers.name: Jim Barry Wines
producers.why: Founded in 1959; The Armagh Shiraz, the Florita vineyard Riesling from Watervale and a long record of Cabernet Malbec.

producers.name: Wendouree
producers.why: Founded at Sevenhill in 1895 and still farming vines from that era; dense, tannic, decades-lived Shiraz, Cabernet Malbec and Shiraz Mataro, sold by mailing list.

producers.name: Sevenhill Cellars
producers.why: The Jesuit winery founded in 1851, the valley's oldest, still making altar wine beside its table wines.

producers.name: Kilikanoon
producers.why: A modern house known for powerful Shiraz and Grenache and a run of show trophies.

producers.name: Taylors
producers.why: The valley's largest family house, planted in 1969 beside the Wakefield River; sold as Wakefield abroad, strong in Cabernet, Shiraz and Riesling.

producers.name: Mount Horrocks
producers.why: A Watervale house named for the valley's 1840 pioneer, known for Riesling and for a Cordon Cut dessert Riesling made by cutting the canes to raisin the fruit on the vine.

producers.name: Pikes
producers.why: A Polish Hill River house whose Rieslings show the district's slate and whose reds are generous.

exam: Place Clare in the Mount Lofty Ranges zone, 130 kilometres north of Adelaide, at 400 to 500 metres, and keep it out of the Barossa zone.
Give the Riesling style in five words: bone dry, lime, slate, high acid, screwcap, and the 2000 vintage as the year the valley switched.
Set Watervale against Polish Hill River: red loam over limestone and floral lime against slate and flint.
Name the reds: firm minty Shiraz and the Cabernet Malbec blend, with Wendouree and Jim Barry as the keepers.
Know the founding dates: first vines 1840 at Penwortham, Sevenhill by the Jesuits in 1851, Wendouree 1895.
At Advanced, map the sub-districts south to north and know the Adelaide Hills subregions, Piccadilly Valley and Lenswood, as the zone's cool cousins.
traps: Clare is not in the Barossa zone; it is a region of the Mount Lofty Ranges zone with the Adelaide Hills and Adelaide Plains.
The TERROIR row pairs Eden and Clare for Riesling, but they are in different zones and 100 kilometres apart; Eden is Barossa's hill country, Clare stands alone to the north.
Clare Riesling is dry by default; the toast and honey of an old bottle come from age, not oak or sugar.
Watervale and Polish Hill River are districts, not registered subregions; Polish Hill is a vineyard name on one house's label.
The screwcap switch was the 2000 vintage, led by thirteen Clare Riesling makers, not a government rule and not a Barossa idea.
The Cabernet partner in old Clare blends is Malbec, not Shiraz or Merlot.

cards.f: Clare Valley: zone, distance and height
cards.b: Mount Lofty Ranges zone (with Adelaide Hills and Adelaide Plains), about 130 kilometres north of Adelaide, vineyards at 400 to 550 metres with hot days and cold nights.

cards.f: Clare Riesling in five words
cards.b: Bone dry, lime, slate, high acid, screwcap. Alcohol 11.5 to 13 per cent, no oak, no malolactic; toast and honey after ten years in bottle.

cards.f: Watervale against Polish Hill River
cards.b: Watervale: red loam over limestone, floral lime, rounder, earlier. Polish Hill River: slatey shale over clay, flinty, austere, slower to age. Grosset's Springvale and Polish Hill show the pair.

cards.f: The screwcap vintage and who led it
cards.b: The 2000 vintage: thirteen Clare Valley Riesling producers bottled under screwcap together, and the rest of Australia followed within a few years.

cards.f: Clare's old red blend
cards.b: Cabernet Sauvignon with Malbec, a nineteenth-century habit kept by Wendouree and Jim Barry; firm, minty, long-lived.

cards.f: Clare founding dates
cards.b: First vines 1840 at Penwortham; Sevenhill Cellars by the Jesuits 1851, the valley's oldest winery; Wendouree 1895; Taylors 1969; Grosset 1981.

cards.f: The Armagh: whose wine, what grape, where
cards.b: Jim Barry Wines' flagship Shiraz, from the Armagh hamlet west of the town of Clare; first vintage 1985.

cards.f: Clare sub-districts south to north
cards.b: Auburn, Watervale, Penwortham, Sevenhill, Clare (with Armagh to the west); Polish Hill River lies in a side valley to the east. None is a registered subregion.

questions.q: In which zone does the Clare Valley region lie?
questions.exp: Clare Valley shares the Mount Lofty Ranges zone with the Adelaide Hills and Adelaide Plains; it lies outside the Barossa zone, a frequent exam trap, while Limestone Coast holds Coonawarra and South West Australia is Margaret River's zone.

questions.q: Which Clare sub-district gives the softer, more floral lime Riesling on red loam over limestone?
questions.exp: Watervale, in the south-centre, sits on red loam over limestone with shale and gives the rounder, lime-blossom style; Polish Hill River, on hard slatey shale to the east, gives the flintier, more austere, slower-ageing Riesling.

questions.q: For which vintage did Clare's Riesling makers bottle under screwcap together, leading Australia?
questions.exp: Thirteen Clare Valley producers put their 2000 Rieslings under screwcap to end cork taint and random oxidation; within a few years screwcap became the national norm for white wine.

questions.q: Which religious order founded Sevenhill Cellars in 1851?
questions.exp: Austrian Jesuits founded Sevenhill in 1851 to make sacramental wine, and the winery still does; it is the oldest in the Clare Valley.

questions.q: What is the name of Jim Barry's flagship Clare Valley Shiraz?
questions.exp: The Armagh is named for the hamlet west of the town of Clare where it is grown; its first vintage was 1985 and it sits among Australia's most collected Shiraz.

questions.q: How is a typical Clare Valley Riesling finished for sweetness?
questions.exp: Clare Riesling is fermented to dryness with no oak or malolactic conversion, at 11.5 to 13 per cent alcohol; an off-dry or late-harvest version is the exception and says so on the label.

questions.q: Which red blend is a Clare Valley tradition at houses such as Wendouree and Jim Barry?
questions.exp: Cabernet Malbec goes back to the nineteenth century in Clare, Malbec adding plum and softness to firm Cabernet; Cabernet Shiraz is the wider South Australian pairing and Grenache Mataro a Barossa one.

regions.name: McLaren Vale (SA)
regions.summary: McLaren Vale lies half an hour south of Adelaide in the Fleurieu zone, a bowl of vineyards between the Mount Lofty Ranges and the beaches of Gulf St Vincent, warm in the Mediterranean way but cooled every afternoon by the sea breeze. Vines were planted at Reynella in 1838 and Thomas Hardy bought Tintara in 1876, so it is among the oldest regions in the country and has never seen phylloxera. Shiraz leads, dark, savoury and chocolatey with a saline tang, and old bush-vine Grenache is the second claim, alone or in the GSM blend with Mataro. The geology is famously diverse, more than forty mapped units, and Fiano, Vermentino, Tempranillo and Nero d’Avola are the modern experiment.

terroir.climate: Warm Mediterranean with a maritime brake: hot dry summers, mild wet winters with 550 to 650 millimetres of rain, and an afternoon sea breeze off Gulf St Vincent that drops the temperature and keeps acid in the fruit. Frost is almost unknown and rot pressure is low. Sites climb from sea level to over 300 metres at Clarendon, so harvest dates spread across March and April and a cool hill block and a warm sandy one can be weeks apart.
terroir.soils: The region's boast and its geologists' delight: more than forty distinct geological units mapped across a small area, from ancient rock to recent sand. Blewitt Springs has deep, pale sands over clay that suit Grenache bush vines; McLaren Flat and the central floor sit on alluvial loams; Willunga and the Sellicks foothills on red-brown earths over limestone and ironstone; Clarendon on older, rockier hill soils. The variety is the argument behind the region's single-site Shiraz.
terroir.topography: A broad amphitheatre opening west to the gulf, the Willunga escarpment and the Sellicks Hill Range forming its eastern and southern wall, the Onkaparinga River gorge its northern edge, and the land stepping down from Clarendon and Kangarilla in the hills through Blewitt Springs and McLaren Flat to Willunga, Aldinga and the coast.
terroir.water: Gulf St Vincent gives the afternoon breeze and the saline note tasters find in the Shiraz; the Onkaparinga River bounds the north. Irrigation leans on treated, recycled water piped from Adelaide through a regional scheme, a practical answer to a dry summer that the region has used since the end of the 1990s.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Full-bodied with blackberry, plum and dark chocolate, a savoury, almost salty edge and softer tannin than the Barossa; the region's identity and the subject of its single-vineyard Scarce Earth bottlings.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: Old bush vines on sand, some planted in the 1940s, giving perfumed raspberry and red cherry, sandy tannin and mid-weight charm; now made with whole bunches and old wood, and the region's fastest-rising wine.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Ripe blackcurrant and dark chocolate, softer and warmer than Coonawarra, alone or with Shiraz and Merlot in blends such as Church Block.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.styles: Mataro from old vines, meaty, dark and firm, the M of the GSM blend and occasionally bottled alone.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: Among the Mediterranean varieties that suit the warm dry summer, giving cherry, leather and moderate tannin.

grapes.name: Fiano
grapes.styles: A southern Italian white, textural, honeyed and herbal, that keeps its acid in heat better than Chardonnay and has become a regional signature white.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.styles: Crisp, saline and citrus-led, a summer white for the beaches an hour from the vineyards.

grapes.name: Nero d’Avola
grapes.styles: Sicily's red, dark-fruited and spicy, planted for its ease in heat.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Grown mostly in the cooler hills around Clarendon and Kangarilla for a ripe, peachy white.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.styles: Australia's first commercial planting was here in 1985; savoury, cherry-led and medium-bodied.

wines.note: Full-bodied and generous, blackberry, plum, dark chocolate and liquorice with a savoury, faintly salty finish and soft, round tannin; mostly French oak now. Serve just below room temperature with braised beef, barbecued lamb or a mushroom ragù.

From old bush vines on sand: raspberry, red cherry, rose and dried herbs, mid-weight with fine sandy tannin and little new oak, like a sunny Châteauneuf without the weight. Serve slightly cool with roast pork, duck or charcuterie.
Grenache, Shiraz and Mataro, the southern Rhône model: spice, red and black fruit, earth and warmth, friendly young and good with lamb, sausages and grilled vegetables.
Ripe blackcurrant and chocolate with a eucalypt lift and soft tannin, rounder than Coonawarra's; often blended with Shiraz and Merlot.
Textural and dry, pear, honeysuckle and almond with firm acid, the region's modern white for seafood, grilled fish and salty antipasti.

made.viticulture: Vines run from old bush vines on sand, dry grown and hand picked, to modern trellised blocks under drip irrigation and machine harvest. The region pioneered the use of recycled water for irrigation and its growers wrote the sustainability programme that grew into the national scheme for Australian vineyards, so cover crops, reduced spraying and water accounting are regional habits rather than novelties. Heat is the main hazard: a summer spike can shrivel Shiraz and push alcohol past 15 per cent, so canopies are kept full for shade and picking has moved earlier over the last two decades. Grenache is picked for perfume rather than weight, and whole bunches are kept for the ferment. The old trunk disease Eutypa, which kills one arm of a vine and leaves the other bearing, is common on old Shiraz and gave d'Arenberg's flagship its name, The Dead Arm. Phylloxera has never arrived, so vines are on their own roots. Site matters more each year: Blewitt Springs for Grenache on sand, Clarendon for cooler, later Shiraz and Chardonnay in the hills, Willunga and Seaview for the fuller, warmer styles.
made.winemaking: Shiraz is made in open fermenters with pump-overs or foot treading at the traditional houses, pressed in basket presses at d'Arenberg and a few others, and matured in French oak hogsheads and puncheons for twelve to twenty months; the American oak of the past has mostly gone. The best makers hold alcohol near 14 to 14.5 per cent by picking on flavour and blending across sites. The Scarce Earth programme bottles single-vineyard Shiraz from named sites, tasted and approved by a regional panel, so the geology can be compared glass by glass. Grenache has been remade: whole-bunch and whole-berry ferments, gentle extraction, ageing in old barrels, concrete or large vats, and no new oak, to keep the raspberry perfume and sandy tannin. GSM blends are assembled from separate parcels. The Mediterranean whites, Fiano and Vermentino, are fermented cool in stainless steel, sometimes with skin contact or lees for texture, and bottled dry under screwcap. A handful of houses make traditional-method sparkling Shiraz, dark, sweet-edged and a Christmas tradition.

law.classification: McLaren Vale is a registered region of the Fleurieu zone, which also holds Langhorne Creek, Currency Creek, Southern Fleurieu and Kangaroo Island. The GI is a line on the map and no more; the 85 per cent rule for variety, vintage and origin applies. The districts a server meets on labels, Blewitt Springs, Clarendon, McLaren Flat, Seaview, Willunga and the rest, are growers' names used by the regional association, not registered subregions. Scarce Earth is a regional programme for single-site Shiraz with its own tasting panel, a private mark; sustainability certification is likewise voluntary. Several of the region's Shiraz and Grenache wines sit in Langton's private classification.
tiers: Zone: Fleurieu
The peninsula zone south of Adelaide: McLaren Vale, Langhorne Creek, Currency Creek, Southern Fleurieu and Kangaroo Island.
Region: McLaren Vale
The registered GI from the Onkaparinga River south to Sellicks; 85 per cent of a McLaren Vale wine comes from inside the line.
Districts (unofficial)
Blewitt Springs, Clarendon, Kangarilla, McLaren Flat, Seaview, Willunga, Sellicks Foothills, Aldinga and others, used by growers and on labels, none registered as a subregion.
labels: Scarce Earth

GSM
