places.name: Blewitt Springs
places.note: The elevated northern district on deep sand over clay, cooler than the floor and the heartland of old bush-vine Grenache, with some vines from the 1940s; fine, perfumed Shiraz too.

places.name: Clarendon
places.note: The hill district in the north-east above 300 metres, the coolest part of the region, giving later-picked Shiraz with more pepper and acid, and the region's best Chardonnay.

places.name: McLaren Flat
places.note: The alluvial centre east of the township, generous Shiraz and Grenache on loam and sand.

places.name: Seaview
places.note: The ridge west of the township towards the gulf, with ironstone and limestone, named for the old Seaview winery that stood there; ripe, saline Shiraz.

places.name: Willunga
places.note: The southern town beneath the escarpment, warm red-brown earths over limestone and the site of the regional farmers' market; full-bodied Shiraz and Cabernet.

places.name: Reynella
places.note: The northern gateway near the Onkaparinga where the first vines went in in 1838 and where the Hardy company kept its historic home.

places.name: The Fleurieu zone beyond McLaren Vale
places.note: The zone's four other regions lie east and south; a server meets Langhorne Creek on lists most often.

places.name: Langhorne Creek
places.note: East of the Mount Lofty Ranges near Lake Alexandrina, a flat region once irrigated by the winter flooding of the Bremer River, cooled by lake breezes, known for soft, generous Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz that fed many blends.

places.name: Currency Creek
places.note: Between Langhorne Creek and the Southern Ocean near Goolwa, maritime and modest, with Cabernet and Shiraz.

places.name: Southern Fleurieu
places.note: The cool, windy southern tip of the peninsula on Encounter Bay, with Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Kangaroo Island
places.note: The island off the peninsula's tip, maritime and small in vineyard, with Bordeaux varieties and Shiraz.

producers.name: d'Arenberg
producers.why: Founded in 1912 and still foot treading and basket pressing; The Dead Arm Shiraz, a long list of oddly named wines and a cube-shaped cellar door made it the region's best-known name.

producers.name: Hardys Tintara
producers.why: Thomas Hardy bought the Tintara winery in 1876, and the company he founded in 1853 became one of Australia's largest; Tintara remains its McLaren Vale home.

producers.name: Wirra Wirra
producers.why: Founded in 1894 and revived in 1969; Church Block, a Cabernet Shiraz Merlot blend, is one of Australia's best-loved everyday reds, and RSW Shiraz its flagship.

producers.name: Kay Brothers Amery
producers.why: A family winery of 1890 whose Block 6 Shiraz comes from vines planted in 1892, among the oldest in the region.

producers.name: Coriole
producers.why: Planted Australia's first commercial Sangiovese in 1985 and leads the region's Italian turn with Fiano and Nero d'Avola beside its old-vine Shiraz.

producers.name: Yangarra Estate
producers.why: A biodynamic estate at Blewitt Springs whose High Sands Grenache, from bush vines planted in 1946, is the reference for the modern style.

producers.name: Chapel Hill
producers.why: A house named for its 1865 stone chapel, known for balanced Shiraz, Grenache and Mediterranean whites.

exam: Place McLaren Vale in the Fleurieu zone south of Adelaide on Gulf St Vincent, and name the sea breeze as its climate.
Give Shiraz as the lead and old bush-vine Grenache as the second claim, and spell out GSM as Grenache, Shiraz, Mataro.
Know the geology as the region's boast, more than forty units, and Blewitt Springs' sand as the Grenache district.
Name the founding facts: Reynella 1838, Hardy's Tintara 1876, d'Arenberg 1912, and no phylloxera.
Recognise the Mediterranean varieties, Fiano, Vermentino, Tempranillo and Nero d'Avola, as the region's modern direction.
At Advanced, list the Fleurieu zone's other regions and know Langhorne Creek's Cabernet and Bremer River flooding.
traps: McLaren Vale is in the Fleurieu zone, not the Mount Lofty Ranges zone, though the ranges form its eastern wall.
Mataro is Mourvèdre; GSM is Grenache, Shiraz and Mataro in descending order, not a fixed recipe.
The districts, Blewitt Springs and the rest, are unofficial; the region has no registered subregion.
McLaren Vale Shiraz is savoury and chocolatey with a saline edge, softer than Barossa, warmer than Coonawarra; do not call it jammy by default.
The Dead Arm is a Shiraz named for a vine disease, Eutypa dieback, not for a style or a vineyard.
Scarce Earth is a regional single-vineyard programme with a tasting panel, not a classification in law.

cards.b: Fleurieu zone, south of Adelaide between the Mount Lofty Ranges and Gulf St Vincent; warm Mediterranean with a daily sea breeze, almost no frost, 550 to 650 millimetres of winter rain.

cards.b: Full-bodied, blackberry, plum and dark chocolate with a savoury, saline edge and soft tannin; French oak now, about 14 to 14.5 per cent.

cards.f: GSM: the grapes and the order
cards.b: Grenache, Shiraz, Mataro (Mourvèdre), named in descending order of proportion; the southern Rhône model from old South Australian bush vines.

cards.f: Blewitt Springs: soil and grape
cards.b: Deep pale sand over clay in the elevated north of McLaren Vale; the heartland of old bush-vine Grenache, some planted in the 1940s, and fine perfumed Shiraz.

cards.f: McLaren Vale founding dates
cards.b: First vines at Reynella 1838; Hardy founded 1853 and bought Tintara 1876; Kay Brothers 1890; Wirra Wirra 1894; d'Arenberg 1912. Never any phylloxera.

cards.f: The Fleurieu zone's five regions
cards.b: McLaren Vale, Langhorne Creek, Currency Creek, Southern Fleurieu and Kangaroo Island.

cards.f: The Dead Arm: house, grape, name
cards.b: d'Arenberg's flagship Shiraz, named for Eutypa dieback, the trunk disease that kills one arm of an old vine and concentrates the crop on the other.

cards.f: McLaren Vale's Mediterranean varieties
cards.b: Fiano and Vermentino for whites, Tempranillo, Nero d'Avola and Sangiovese for reds; Coriole planted the first commercial Sangiovese in Australia in 1985.

questions.q: In which zone does the McLaren Vale region lie?
questions.exp: McLaren Vale is a region of the Fleurieu zone on the peninsula south of Adelaide, with Langhorne Creek, Currency Creek, Southern Fleurieu and Kangaroo Island; the Mount Lofty Ranges zone holds Clare and the Adelaide Hills.

questions.q: Which three grapes make up a GSM blend?
questions.exp: GSM is Grenache, Shiraz and Mataro, the Australian name for Mourvèdre, in descending order of proportion; it follows the southern Rhône's Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre.

questions.q: Which body of water sends the afternoon breeze that cools McLaren Vale?
questions.exp: The gulf west of Adelaide lies at the region's feet; its afternoon breeze drops the summer temperature, keeps acid in the fruit and gives the Shiraz its saline note.

questions.q: Which McLaren Vale district, on deep sands, is the heartland of old bush-vine Grenache?
questions.exp: Blewitt Springs' pale sand over clay in the elevated north grows the region's finest Grenache, some vines from the 1940s; Clarendon is the cool hill district and the Sellicks Foothills the warm south.

questions.q: After which vine disorder is d'Arenberg's flagship Shiraz, The Dead Arm, named?
questions.exp: Eutypa dieback is a trunk disease that kills one arm of an old vine and leaves the other to carry a small, concentrated crop; the two mildews are leaf and bunch diseases, and phylloxera has never reached South Australia.

questions.q: Where were McLaren Vale's first vines planted in 1838?
questions.exp: Vines went in at Reynella, the region's northern gateway near the Onkaparinga River, in 1838, which makes McLaren Vale among Australia's oldest regions; Thomas Hardy's purchase of Tintara followed in 1876, and phylloxera has never arrived.

questions.q: Which Fleurieu region east of the ranges was traditionally irrigated by the winter flooding of the Bremer River?
questions.exp: Langhorne Creek near Lake Alexandrina diverted the Bremer's winter floods across its flat vineyards, growing soft, generous Cabernet and Shiraz that fed many South Australian blends.

questions.q: Which historic McLaren Vale winery did Thomas Hardy buy in 1876?
questions.exp: Hardy bought Tintara in 1876 and made it the McLaren Vale home of the company he had founded in 1853; Reynella is where the first vines of 1838 were planted and Amery is the Kay Brothers' 1890 estate.

regions.name: Coonawarra (SA)
regions.summary: Coonawarra is a flat, cool strip in the south-eastern corner of South Australia, near the Victorian border and some 60 to 70 kilometres from the Southern Ocean, in the Limestone Coast zone. Its fame rests on one soil, terra rossa, a red-brown loam over soft porous limestone over a shallow water table, along a low ancient dune ridge about 20 kilometres long and two wide, running north from Penola. On it Cabernet Sauvignon ripens slowly into blackcurrant, mint and cedar with firm acid and fine tannin, the most structured Cabernet in Australia and the exam’s answer to Bordeaux. John Riddoch planted the colony in 1890, Wynns gave it its label in 1951, and the vines are on their own roots.

terroir.climate: Cool to moderate and maritime for Australia: the Southern Ocean lies some 60 to 70 kilometres west and a cold offshore upwelling sends cloud and breeze across the flat land through the summer afternoons, so the growing season is long and the harvest late, running into April and May. Winter rain of around 600 millimetres falls outside the season, summers are dry, and the two risks are spring frost on the open plain and rain at the tail of a late vintage. The heat summation is close to Bordeaux's.
terroir.soils: Terra rossa: a friable red-brown loam, 30 to 100 centimetres deep, coloured by iron oxide, lying over soft white limestone of an ancient coastal ridge, with a water table a metre or two below. It drains freely yet the roots reach moisture, so the vine is neither stressed nor flooded. Flanking it on lower ground are heavier black rendzina soils over the same limestone, cooler, wetter and less prized, which the boundary argument was about.
terroir.topography: Almost perfectly flat at about 60 metres above sea level, the terra rossa strip is a barely perceptible ridge of old dune limestone running north from Penola past the hamlet of Coonawarra, roughly 20 kilometres long and two kilometres across. There are no slopes to speak of; aspect means nothing here and soil means everything.
terroir.water: No river runs through it. The limestone holds an aquifer that sits a metre or two beneath the terra rossa, which the vines drink from and the growers draw for drip irrigation and for the overhead sprinklers that fight spring frost. The Southern Ocean to the west supplies the cloud and the cool.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The grape of the strip: blackcurrant, mulberry, mint and eucalypt, cedar and tobacco with age, firm acid, fine dusty tannin and moderate alcohol near 13.5 to 14.5 per cent; the most age-worthy Cabernet in Australia.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The region's first great grape, planted before Cabernet took over: medium to full, red and black fruit, pepper and mint, cooler and more elegant than Barossa.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: A blending partner for Cabernet and occasionally a varietal, plummy and leafy.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: A seasoning in Bordeaux-style blends, adding perfume and a leafy lift.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.styles: A small part of some blends for colour, violet and tannin in the long cool season.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: A minor partner in Cabernet blends, as in Lindeman's Pyrus, and rarely bottled alone.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: A secondary white, citrus and stone fruit with good acid from the cool season.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Once a regional strength and still made dry and limey by a few houses, lighter than Clare's.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: A crisp, grassy white in small quantity for the cellar door.

wines.note: Blackcurrant, mulberry and mint with cedar and a eucalypt lift, medium to full in body, firm acid and fine, dusty tannin; it is structured and savoury, never jammy, and the best keep twenty years. Decant young ones; roast lamb, beef with a bordelaise sauce, aged hard cheese.
Medium to full, red and black fruit with pepper, spice and mint, firmer and cooler than Barossa; Penfolds Bin 128 and Wynns' Michael are the names. Duck, pork, game birds.

The classic South Australian blend done in Coonawarra's cooler key: Cabernet's structure with Shiraz's flesh, as in Majella's The Malleea; Lindeman's Limestone Ridge names Shiraz first because Shiraz leads it, since the first grape named is the larger share.
Dry, light and limey from the cool season, a reminder of the region's white past, drunk young with oysters and fish.
Citrus and white peach with lively acid and light oak, the cool flat land's secondary white.

made.viticulture: The flat land and the even soil made Coonawarra the laboratory of Australian vineyard mechanisation: machine harvesting was adopted early, and machine and minimal pruning were taken up early, so many blocks are hedged and picked by machine, with hand work kept for the oldest vines and the flagship blocks. Vines are on their own roots because South Australia has never had phylloxera, and a little Shiraz dates from the 1890s plantings and much of the Cabernet from the revival of the 1950s and 1960s. Spring frost is the great hazard on the open plain, fought with overhead sprinklers fed from the limestone aquifer; cool, cloudy seasons can also delay ripening into May, when rain may arrive, so canopies are opened to let light in and picking is by flavour and tannin rather than sugar. Drip irrigation is modest, because the roots reach the water table. The fight over the boundary ran through the 1990s and ended in the early 2000s with a GI wider than the red strip alone, so a Coonawarra label does not promise terra rossa, and the serious houses say which soil a wine stands on.
made.winemaking: Cabernet is fermented in stainless steel or open vats with cool, measured extraction, a short post-ferment maceration to fix the tannin, and twelve to twenty-four months in French oak barriques and hogsheads, with new oak held to a share that lets blackcurrant and mint stay in front; a few houses keep American oak for Shiraz. Blends with Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot or Malbec are assembled before bottling, and the Cabernet Shiraz pairing is the region's South Australian inheritance. The wines are released young and are meant to age: the structure softens into cedar, tobacco and dried mint over ten to twenty years. Wynns' Black Label Cabernet has been made every year since 1954 and its John Riddoch since 1982, and the pair define the two styles, the regional blend and the single top-block selection. Riesling and Chardonnay are made simply, cool fermented in steel, the Chardonnay with a little barrel, and bottled dry under screwcap.

law.classification: Coonawarra is a registered region of the Limestone Coast zone, which also holds Padthaway, Wrattonbully, Mount Benson, Robe and Mount Gambier, each registered separately. Its boundary was the most contested in Australia: growers on the black soil argued their way into the GI through the 1990s and the line fixed in the early 2000s is wider than the terra rossa strip, so the GI promises origin, not soil. Within it, the 85 per cent rule for variety, vintage and region applies and no grape or style is prescribed. Terra rossa itself is a soil name with no legal standing, and John Riddoch, Black Label and Bin 128 are house terms. Langton's lists several Coonawarra Cabernets, privately.
tiers: Zone: Limestone Coast
The south-eastern corner of South Australia: Coonawarra, Wrattonbully, Padthaway, Mount Benson, Robe and Mount Gambier.
Region: Coonawarra
The registered GI around and beyond the terra rossa strip from Penola northward; 85 per cent of the wine from inside the line, with no promise of soil.
Terra rossa
A soil, not a tier: the red loam over limestone that gives the famous Cabernet, covering only part of the GI.
labels: Black Label
Wynns Coonawarra Estate's regional Cabernet Sauvignon, made every vintage since 1954; a house term.
John Riddoch
Wynns' top Cabernet from selected blocks, first made in 1982, named for the colony's 1890 founder; a house term.
Bin 128
Penfolds' Coonawarra Shiraz, a single-region wine in the Bin series, unlike the multi-region Bins; a house code.
The Coonawarra Trio
Lindeman's three reds: St George, a single-vineyard Cabernet, Limestone Ridge Shiraz Cabernet and Pyrus, a Bordeaux-style blend; house terms.

places.name: Penola
places.note: The town at the southern end of the strip, founded in the 1850s, where John Riddoch's fruit colony of 1890 began; the service town of the region and the start of the terra rossa.

places.name: Coonawarra village and the strip
places.note: The hamlet in the middle of the terra rossa ridge beside Riddoch's triple-gabled 1890s winery, now Wynns'; the land north to the old cellars is the historic core of Cabernet and Shiraz.

places.name: The Limestone Coast zone beyond Coonawarra
places.note: Five sibling regions on the same limestone, each registered separately; a server meets Padthaway and Wrattonbully most often.

places.name: Wrattonbully
places.note: Immediately north of Coonawarra on the same ridge, with terra rossa of its own and a gentle rise; Cabernet and Shiraz from vineyards largely planted in the 1990s.

places.name: Padthaway
places.note: Further north, warmer and drier, planted by the big companies from the 1960s with terra rossa patches; strong in Chardonnay and Shiraz for blends.

places.name: Mount Benson
places.note: On the coast west of Coonawarra, cooler and windier, with maritime Shiraz and Cabernet from the 1990s.

places.name: Robe
places.note: The coastal region around the fishing town of Robe, next to Mount Benson, small and maritime, with Shiraz, Cabernet and Sauvignon Blanc.

places.name: Mount Gambier
places.note: The southernmost and coolest region near the volcanic lakes, with Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc.

producers.name: Wynns Coonawarra Estate
producers.why: The house the Wynn family bought in 1951 around Riddoch's 1890s winery; Black Label Cabernet since 1954 and John Riddoch since 1982 are the region's measuring sticks.

producers.name: Penfolds
producers.why: Bin 128 is its Coonawarra Shiraz, and Coonawarra Cabernet has long anchored Bin 707; the house proves the strip's place in the South Australian blends.

producers.name: Lindeman's
producers.why: Its Coonawarra Trio, St George, Limestone Ridge and Pyrus, showed from the 1970s that the region could make three serious reds in one cellar.

producers.name: Katnook Estate
producers.why: Built around Riddoch's original woolshed and winery, a leading estate for Cabernet and a Shiraz called Prodigy.

producers.name: Majella
producers.why: A grower family that turned to its own label in 1991; its Cabernet and The Malleea Cabernet Shiraz are among the region's most reliable.

producers.name: Parker Coonawarra Estate
producers.why: Known for its Terra Rossa First Growth Cabernet, a name that borrows Bordeaux's language for the strip's best fruit.

producers.name: Brand's Laira
producers.why: An old vineyard of the strip, with Shiraz vines dating to the 1890s, still labelled for the site.

exam: Place Coonawarra in the Limestone Coast zone in South Australia's far south-east near the Victorian border, and give its climate as cool maritime, moderated by the Southern Ocean.
Define terra rossa: red-brown loam over soft limestone over a shallow water table, on a strip about 20 kilometres long and two wide, running north from Penola.
Give Cabernet Sauvignon as the grape and describe the wine: blackcurrant, mint and cedar, firm acid, fine tannin, never jammy, built to age.
Know the names: John Riddoch's 1890 colony, Wynns from 1951, Black Label since 1954, John Riddoch since 1982, Penfolds Bin 128.
Explain why the GI is wider than the soil: the boundary dispute of the 1990s ended with black soil inside the line.
At Advanced, list the Limestone Coast's six regions and know Wrattonbully as the terra rossa neighbour to the north and Padthaway as the big companies' northern vineyard.
traps: Coonawarra is cool for Australia and flat: its Cabernet is structured and minty, not jammy, and there are no hillsides to talk about.
Terra rossa is red loam over limestone, not volcanic soil, and it covers only part of the GI; a Coonawarra label does not promise it.
Coonawarra lies in the Limestone Coast zone, not Fleurieu or Mount Lofty Ranges, and it is in South Australia, not Victoria, though the border is minutes away.
Shiraz came first and is still serious here; Cabernet overtook it only in the 1960s and 1970s.
The region has no river: its water is the limestone aquifer and the cloud off the Southern Ocean.
Wynns' John Riddoch is a Cabernet from selected blocks and Michael is its Shiraz; Black Label is the regional Cabernet, not a lesser wine of another house.

cards.f: Coonawarra: zone, position and climate
cards.b: Limestone Coast zone, far south-east South Australia near the Victorian border, some 60 to 70 kilometres from the Southern Ocean; cool maritime, cloudy afternoons, late harvest into April and May, spring frost risk.

cards.f: Terra rossa: define it
cards.b: Friable red-brown loam, 30 to 100 centimetres deep, coloured by iron oxide, over soft porous limestone over a water table a metre or two down; free draining yet never dry.

cards.f: The Coonawarra strip: shape and size
cards.b: A flat ridge of old dune limestone about 20 kilometres long and two kilometres wide, running north from Penola through the hamlet of Coonawarra; the cigar on the map.

cards.f: Coonawarra Cabernet in one line
cards.b: Blackcurrant, mulberry, mint and eucalypt with cedar and tobacco in age; firm acid, fine dusty tannin, moderate alcohol, twenty years of life. Australia's most structured Cabernet.

cards.f: Coonawarra dates and names
cards.b: John Riddoch's Penola Fruit Colony 1890 and his triple-gabled winery of the 1890s; the Wynn family bought it in 1951; Black Label Cabernet since 1954; John Riddoch since 1982.

cards.f: Why the Coonawarra GI is wider than its soil
cards.b: A boundary dispute through the 1990s, settled in the early 2000s, brought growers on the flanking black rendzina soil inside the line; the GI promises origin, not terra rossa.

cards.f: The Limestone Coast's six regions
cards.b: Coonawarra, Wrattonbully (just north, terra rossa too), Padthaway (further north, the big companies), Mount Benson and Robe (on the coast), Mount Gambier (south, coolest).

cards.f: Penfolds Bin 128 and Bin 707
cards.b: Bin 128 is Penfolds' Coonawarra Shiraz, one of the few single-region wines in the Bin series; Bin 707 is its flagship Cabernet, a multi-region blend in which Coonawarra fruit has long been central.

questions.q: In which zone does the Coonawarra region lie?
questions.exp: Coonawarra is one of six regions in the Limestone Coast zone of south-eastern South Australia, with Wrattonbully, Padthaway, Mount Benson, Robe and Mount Gambier.

questions.q: What is the name of the red loam over limestone on which Coonawarra's famous Cabernet grows?
questions.exp: Terra rossa, red earth, is a friable iron-rich loam over soft porous limestone with a shallow water table beneath; it covers a strip about 20 kilometres long and two wide.

questions.q: Which grape variety is the most planted in Coonawarra?
questions.exp: Cabernet Sauvignon overtook Shiraz in the 1960s and 1970s and now defines the region; Cabernet Franc is only a blending seasoning and Pinot Noir belongs to cooler Mount Gambier.

questions.q: Which house's label shows the triple-gabled winery John Riddoch built in the 1890s?
questions.exp: The Wynn family bought Riddoch's winery in 1951 and put its three gables on the label of Wynns Coonawarra Estate; Black Label Cabernet has been made there since 1954.

questions.q: Which town at the southern end of the terra rossa strip gave John Riddoch's 1890 fruit colony its name?
questions.exp: Riddoch founded the Penola Fruit Colony in 1890 and the strip runs north from the town; the hamlet of Coonawarra, further up the ridge, later gave the region its name.

questions.q: About how long is the terra rossa strip of Coonawarra?
questions.exp: The strip is about 20 kilometres long and two kilometres wide, the cigar shape on every map; about 60 kilometres is roughly the distance to the Southern Ocean.

questions.q: Which body of water moderates Coonawarra's climate?
questions.exp: The Southern Ocean lies some 60 to 70 kilometres west and its cold offshore upwelling sends cloud and breeze over the flat land through summer; the two gulfs cool Adelaide's regions and Bass Strait cools Tasmania and Victoria.

questions.q: Which Limestone Coast region lies immediately north of Coonawarra on the same limestone ridge?
questions.exp: Wrattonbully adjoins Coonawarra's northern end with terra rossa of its own and vineyards mostly planted in the 1990s; Padthaway lies further north and is warmer.
